title: AI Evaluation Metrics for Real Work
description: Move beyond "looks good". Learn concrete evaluation metrics to score AI outputs for accuracy, usefulness, consistency, and safety.

data.text: Teams often deploy AI workflows without measurable quality standards. That creates hidden risk. A simple evaluation framework lets you compare prompts, models, and workflows objectively instead of relying on intuition.
Core metrics every team should track

rows: 1 = mostly wrong, 5 = fully correct and verifiable
Did it actually do what was requested?
Is output easy to understand and act on?
Does quality stay stable across runs?
Does it avoid risky or disallowed output?

items: Create a benchmark set of 20 representative prompts/tasks.
Run current prompt/model version and save outputs.
Score each output against the 5 metrics above.
Calculate average score per metric and total quality score.
Test one change at a time (prompt tweak, model swap, tool addition).
Promote only changes that improve score without increasing risk.

data.title: Avoid vanity metrics
data.text: Fast response time and long answers can look impressive while quality is poor. Prioritize correctness and task completion first, then optimize speed and style.

data.title: Build your first AI scorecard
data.description: Evaluate one existing AI workflow in your work using a simple scorecard.
steps: Pick a recurring workflow (research summary, email drafting, data analysis, etc.).
Score each output from 1-5 on all five metrics.
Identify the weakest metric and improve that first.
Re-run and compare before/after average scores.
data.expectedOutcome: You end with a measurable quality baseline and a repeatable improvement loop.

data.text: No single metric captures quality. Evaluation should align with impact: higher-risk use cases need stricter thresholds, clearer failure definitions, and human review coverage metrics.

rows: Minimum pass rate plus spot audits
Strict thresholds and mandatory human sign-off

data.caption: A repeatable evaluation loop keeps AI quality from drifting over time.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
  A[Define benchmark tasks] --> B[Run current version]
  B --> C[Score outputs 1-5]
  C --> D[Calculate averages]
  D --> E{Score above threshold?}
  E -->|Yes| F[Promote change]
  E -->|No| G[Revert or iterate]
  G --> B
  F --> H[Monitor production]
  H --> A

cards.title: Factual accuracy
cards.description: Catches hallucinations, wrong dates, fake citations. Most important for any domain where wrong facts cause real harm.

cards.title: Task completion
cards.description: Catches partial outputs, missed requirements, or format violations. Essential for workflows with strict acceptance criteria.

cards.title: Clarity
cards.description: Catches jargon overload, poor structure, or confusing explanations. Critical for customer-facing or training content.

cards.title: Consistency
cards.description: Catches quality drift between runs. Important when the same prompt is reused across a team or production pipeline.

cards.title: Safety/compliance
cards.description: Catches policy violations, biased output, or leaked data. Non-negotiable for regulated industries.

data.title: Concrete evaluation example
data.content:
You run a benchmark of 20 customer-support summary prompts.

Before improvement:
- Factual accuracy: 3.2/5
- Task completion: 3.8/5
- Clarity: 4.1/5
- Consistency: 2.9/5
- Safety: 4.5/5

After adding a system prompt that says 'Only state facts from the provided transcript':
- Factual accuracy: 4.4/5 (+1.2)
- Task completion: 4.0/5 (+0.2)
- Clarity: 4.0/5 (-0.1)
- Consistency: 3.8/5 (+0.9)
- Safety: 4.6/5 (+0.1)

The single biggest win was factual accuracy, which is what the team cared about most.

data.title: Evaluation cheat sheet
points: Always score a baseline before changing prompts or models
Track factual accuracy separately from clarity — they do not always move together
Use the same 20 benchmark prompts for every comparison so results are meaningful
Consistency matters as much as average quality for production systems
Promote only changes that improve your weakest metric without hurting safety

data.title: Avoid vanity metrics
data.text: Fast response time and long answers can look impressive while quality is poor. Prioritize correctness and task completion first, then optimize speed and style.

data.title: Evaluation at a glance
points: Create a benchmark set of 20 representative prompts before any change
Score each output 1-5 on factual accuracy, task completion, clarity, consistency, and safety
Track consistency separately — it is the metric that most often drifts silently
Promote only changes that improve your weakest metric without increasing risk
Re-benchmark every time you change the prompt, model, or tool configuration
